terminal.description: A shell in your workspace where a month of stock changes fills the log, and compaction makes it small again.

tasks.title: Write one record per key
tasks.description:
Implement `store.compact()`: write the log again, one record per key.

- `compact()` writes a new log that holds one record for each key the store holds, with its value, written the way `set` writes it, and no record for a deleted key
- the new log becomes `store.log`; the store's keys and values are the same before and after, and after a restart
- so the new log is exactly as long as the log of a fresh store in which each key was set once

The check never reads the records: it compacts, opens the folder again, and compares the size of `store.log` with a fresh store's log.
nextSteps: Run `node src/try.js` and note how big the log gets.
Build the text of the new log from the keys and values the store holds now.
Write it so that it becomes `store.log`, and run the script again.
hints: Everything a store opened later needs is the last value of each key. Old values and deleted keys are history nobody reads.
The store already holds the last value of every key in memory, and `encode` already writes a set record.
`const text = [...values].map(([key, value]) => encode({ op: 'set', key, value })).join('')` is the whole new log. The next task says how it takes the old one's place.

tasks.title: Swap the new log in, in one step
tasks.description:
Make the new log take the old one's place so that a stop at any moment leaves the whole old log or the whole new one.

- `compact()` writes the new log into `store.log.new`, in the same folder, from the start: a file a stop left under that name is replaced, not added to
- only once that file is whole is it renamed onto `store.log`; afterwards no `store.log.new` is left
- `store.log` itself is never written into, emptied, removed or moved away along the way
- `open` uses only `store.log` and pays no attention to a `store.log.new` it finds

The check keeps a second name for the old log's bytes, to see whether they were written over, notes every call that removes `store.log` or moves it away, and leaves a half-written `store.log.new` from a stop beside the log before it opens your store.
nextSteps: Read "Swapping in one step" in the lesson.
hints: Writing the new log into `store.log` itself means a stop halfway leaves half of it, and the old records are already gone.
`rename` gives a file a new name in one step, and when a file with that name is there, it is replaced in the same step. `writeFile` starts a file from nothing; `appendFile` adds to what is there.
`` await writeFile(`${log}.new`, text) ``, then `` await rename(`${log}.new`, log) ``. No `unlink` before the rename: the rename replaces `store.log` by itself.

tasks.title: Keep going after compaction
tasks.description:
Make the store carry on after `compact()`.

- right after `compact()`, the same store gives every key the value it gave before
- every change after it lands in the new log, the file now called `store.log`
- a store opened later sees the compacted records and every change made after them, around a second `compact()` too

The check compacts, makes changes on the same store, compacts again, closes it and opens the folder again.
nextSteps: Set a key after `compact()` in `node src/try.js`, and check it after the restart.
Think about how your store writes: by the file's name each time, or through something it opened once?
Make sure later changes reach the file that is now `store.log`.
hints: After the rename, the name `store.log` belongs to the new file. Whatever still points at the old file writes into a file nobody will read again.
`appendFile` with a path opens the file by its name each time, so it finds the new one. A file handle opened once keeps pointing at the old file.
If your store keeps a handle from `fs.open`, close it before the rename and open `store.log` again after it, or write with `appendFile(log, ...)` each time.
